en: *Mekhalāṭīkā* on *Kāṇhapāda’s Dohākoṣa*.
Edited by Bagchi (1938), pp. 149ff.;
better edition in *Dhīḥ*, attributed to Amṛtavajra.
Oṃ, homage to the Holder of the Vajra! I bear the pride of the world, yet I am proficient in the ultimate truth; if but one among ten million were to become absorbed in the stainless (nirañjana). 1.

This is its meaning: in the world, one carries pride, thinking, "Who am I? I am proficient in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). And this may be appropriate as long as it is possible. But then, if even one among millions of yogis becomes "merged in the stainless" (*nirañjanalīna*)—that is, one whose mind is merged and submerged in the *sahajakāya*, which is called "stainless" (*nirañjana*) because the "stains" (*añjana*), namely the afflictions such as passion and hatred, have departed from it—and that lord of yogis is like me; such is the sense.
Scholars take pride in the Āgamas, Vedas, and Purāṇas;
like those who have eaten the fruit of the *śirīṣa* tree, they wander about [vainly], having cast out what is false. || 2 ||

This is the meaning: scholars carry the conceit of [realizing] ultimate truth through knowledge derived from external scriptures and so forth. Being of such a nature, what do they do and where? To this he says: just as bees (*alaya*) settle upon ripe *śrīphala* fruits and wander about due to their attachment to the scent, so too, because their vision is obstructed regarding reality by external knowledge such as that of the scriptures, they do not contemplate the nectar-like flavor of the profound reality.
Thus it is said in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*:
"O Great Sage, within the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma..."
Indeed, all those who do not know reality (tattva) are truly rendered fruitless.
He states this proof:
"The Siddha, adorned with wisdom and unshakeable, has been seen by those whose own bodies are naturally pure, like a lotus. (3)

This is the meaning: Bodhicitta is the seminal essence (*śukra*) in the form of conventional vibration, adorned with the female element (*rajas*), and embraced by the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*). To the question "What is the Mind-Vajra?", he says: the *pokkhara* is the lotus-tree to be described; its seed exists by way of the nature of bliss. That very pure Mind-Vajra is seen where? He says: by the word "own" (*nija*), one's own body is meant, which is presided over by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); that itself is understood as being seen in the diagram of the lake. Clarifying this very point, he says: "The sky, water, nectar, mud, and the root-vajra are meditated upon."
When the root-stalk is shaken off, even the "haṃ" sound perishes. || 4 ||

This is the meaning: because it is of the nature of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the sky is *nīra*; Amitābha, the deity of the bliss of bodhicitta, having made the mud, meditates upon the root as the stalk, the primary cause. Producing that very bodhicitta through the sequence of the stalk, petals, and cluster, he says this for that purpose: she is called *avadhūtī* because she shakes off (*dhunoti*) faults such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) without effort (*avahelyā*), that is, effortlessly (*anābhogena*).

The root is fashioned by the *avadhūtī*, which is the primary stalk; thus, the syllable of the word "the cause of the root-stalk fashioned by the *avadhūtī*" refers to the syllable *haṃ*. Furthermore, by means of the form of nectar (*makaranda*) to be described later, the Unstruck (*anāhata*) becomes the Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*) in the form of the syllables of Vajrānaṅga—this is the meaning.

Now, as for what those stalks, leaves, and lotus-fibers rooted in the *avadhūtī* are, he says: *Lalanā, rasanā, ravi, sasi, tuḍiya, veṇṇa—these six are on both sides; they are the four petals, the four stalks, situated in the abode of Great Bliss.* (5)

This is the meaning: in the left nostril, Lalanā resides as the nature of the Moon of Wisdom (prajñā); in the right nostril, Rasanā resides as the nature of the Sun of Skillful Means (upāya). Two neuter channels (ṣaṇḍa) reside in the two sides, that is, in the left and right. And so it is said in the Hevajra Tantra: "Lalanā resides as the nature of Wisdom, and Rasanā as Skillful Means;
Avadhūtī, however, is in the middle region, free from subject and object."

The object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is the knowable (*jñeya*), and the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is knowledge (*jñāna*); she is devoid of these two. In this context, "undivided from duality" means that because there is no absence of error regarding those two—the knowable and knowledge—which stand in the relation of produced and producer, their attainment of substantial existence is excluded; such is the meaning. She is established upon four lotus stalks, which consist of four leaves in the form of the four voids: the void, the exceeding void, the great void, and the universal void, and which themselves consist of the four elements and so forth.

Where? He says: "The abode of great bliss" (*mahāsukhavāsa*) means that which dwells in this [place]; it is the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, the locus of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*), designated as the "Holder of the Net" (*jāladharā*) consisting of the *ḍākinī*-net; the meaning is the peak of Mount Meru.
"In the blossomed lotus of the *evam* syllable, the hero of the gods, in the form of a honeybee, inhales the nectar. (6)

Thus, having taken the seed—the blossoming *aravinda* lotus—through the yoga of the mind-vajra’s wisdom and means in the form of a bee, the Hero (*vīra*) experiences the nectar (*makaranda*), which is the bliss of the mind as unceasing great passion (*mahārāga*). This is because he subdues dispassion (*virāga*) through his heroism in the supreme sexual union of the flower; it means that the Vajra experiences the bliss of the mind as non-falling (*acyuta*) great passion. However, it is not that [the practitioner] himself becomes the object [of experience], producing the fruit through the beginningless sequence [of ordinary perception] and then smelling it. How is this seen in another scripture? Thus, in the *Śrī Hevajra*:

"He is himself the creator, himself the destroyer, himself the king, and himself the Lord. By "himself the destroyer," it is meant that he is the very form of dissolution. By "himself the Lord," it is meant that he possesses sovereignty over all. Like a jewel of universal form (*viśvarūpamaṇi*), his essential nature consists of manifestation, vibration, and withdrawal.
Just as the five great elements, when united in their totality, are joined together—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—[so is he]. (7)

This is the meaning: having taken the seed consisting of the five great elements—the pentad of earth, water, fire, wind, and space—and demonstrating that very [process] through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, he says: "From hardness, the earth is solid; from fluidity, water; from friction, the fire that consumes oblations is born; from space, the wind. Because its nature is bliss, it is space. The meaning is that the body is a complete confluence of the five elements. And as it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"Why is the aggregate (*skandha*) composed of the elements? The Blessed One replied:
Through the union of saliva and spittle, from the touch of that which has the nature of hardness,
earth is produced therein.
From the melting form of the bodhicitta and from the downward movement, fire is produced; from friction, wind is proclaimed to arise;
and bliss is the space element—thus it is established by all five.

This is the meaning: "Therein" means that in the innate (*sahaja*), the earth element arises. *Bola* is the *vajra* and *kakkola* is the *padma*; the intention is [union] through the conjunction of the *vajra* and the *padma*. Therein, in the innate, the bodhicitta is born; the semen (*śukra*) arises. Because it has the nature of the moon, there is the manifestation or arising of water. From friction, fire is born; by the friction of the *vajra* and the *padma*, the fire element arises. Wind is proclaimed to come from space; because its nature is movement, it is proclaimed as the wind element. Bliss and the space element [arise], because their nature is bliss.
In this void, which is filled with the five [senses] and the pleasant fragrance of the celestial breeze, all gods and demons have emerged; yet this very thing is that same void.

This is the meaning: "the sky" is space (*ākāśa*), and "wind" is air (*samīraṇa*); [the phrase] "in their pleasant abode" means in a place of comfort, which is filled with the five great elements (*mahābhūta*). These five are the cause of the origin of all beings, including humans, gods, and asuras. To explain what that very totality of gods and asuras is like, he says: "O fool" (*vaḍhe*)—this is an address using the syllable *vaḍhe*, meaning one who is devoid of this knowledge. This very pentad of elements, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is the fourth, the waveless void, whose form is the innate (*sahaja*)—this is the meaning. And so it is said:
Having reached a certain portion of the salt water, someone perceives the entire ocean as being milk;
likewise, having understood it to be of a single nature in one part, [one concludes so for the whole].
It delimits the entirety of the triple world.

There is another way [of explaining this]: the organ of earth is the nose, and its object is smell; smell exists only in earth and nowhere else. The organ of water is the tongue, and its object is taste; it perceives only taste by necessity. The organ of fire is the eye, and its object is form. The organ of air is the skin, and its object is touch—the objects of touch being the genitals, the penis, and so forth. The organ of space is the ear, and its object is sound; it perceives only sound by necessity and nothing else. Explaining this very point, he says:
Take the earth, water, fire, wind, and sky as your measuring sticks;
having grasped the mandala-chakra, measure it with all-encompassing intelligence. 9.

These very five elements are the object; through the union of the vajra and the lotus, the cognition that arises within them is the "mind of bliss," which is the cognition of the object. Taking hold of that, through instruction from one such as I, you should realize [the truth] extending as far as earth, water, fire, air, and space. By this, he explains what that [state] is like: "Like a waveless ocean, of the nature of the innate (*sahaja*), free from all impurities, devoid of sin and merit, without hunger or thirst—it is clearly explained. (10)

This is the meaning: from the state of waves, one reaches the waveless, even Nirvāṇa, which is the form of the innate (*sahaja*), free from all turbidity, and devoid of the sins of passion and so forth; the meaning is that it is completely abandoned [of such stains]. And thus it was said by the illustrious Ādibuddha:
"There is no sin greater than passion, nor is there any merit greater than bliss.
Therefore, O King, let the mind always be established in imperishable bliss."

And therefore, by this [realization], the triple world should be understood as the waveless, innate form (*sahajarūpa*), because it is composed of the five great elements. And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"Bliss is black, bliss is yellow, bliss is red, bliss is white;
Bliss is blue, bliss is black, bliss is all that is moving and unmoving."

Thus, in such a state, although it is designated as "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*), it is an abiding free from suffering; therein, neither "sin"—which is the suffering of passion and so forth—nor "merit"—which is the pleasure of passion—exists even in the slightest degree. And so it is said in the *Śrī Sampuṭa*: "Abandoning both passion and dispassion, he abides once more. This was clearly stated by Kṛṣṇācārya; the meaning is that this has not been stated by others. Furthermore, for those whose knowledge is turned outward, it is for the sake of engaging with the external self. Showing that "Kṛṣṇa" means dark, variegated, or born of painful hardship, he says:
The Kali age has been cast out by the Vahinī; it is established in both the void and the non-void.
O fool, nothing at all was seen in the midst of those two, the void and the non-void.

This is the meaning: having arranged the wheel of forms through the emptiness of all external phenomena, and having mentally entered even the end of passion within the body—which is not empty—through imagined yoga, then, O fool, nothing whatsoever of the reality that lies between these two, emptiness and non-emptiness, has been seen or known; this is the sense. If one were to say, "In that case, there is no reality at all," he says:
"The innate alone exists as supreme there; perceive it clearly!
Though one reads many scriptures and traditions and hears them, O fool, one knows nothing at all. (12)

This is the meaning: there is one supreme reality, which is the innate (*sahaja*). And that the Supreme One (*para*) alone knows. He reads, teaches, hears, and causes others to hear various scriptures such as logic (*tarka*) and the many kinds of *āgamas* such as the *Kriyā* and *Caryā* tantras; yet he knows nothing at all because he is turned away from the secrets of the unsurpassed Mantra system, such as the Vajrayāna. On the other hand, one like me knows that supreme [reality].
"I do not understand, and I do not go [there]. Devoid of duality, it remains immovable."
Kṛṣṇa says: My mind does not break even in any way;
it remains as steady as the wind-still wife in her home. 13.

This is the meaning: it does not go downward because of the cessation of the *apāna* wind, nor does it go upward because of the cessation of the *prāṇa* wind. Devoid of and abandoned by both—the upward and downward *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds—one remains having expelled the *bodhicitta* in that manner. Demonstrating this very point, he says: Kṛṣṇācārya says "mind" (*mana*), which means the *bodhicitta* does not burst forth in any way and is not obstructed. To clarify where such *bodhicitta* abides, he says:
The excellent mountain caves become deep and all there are shattered;
the pure waters dry up even if the fire of cosmic destruction (kālāgni) should enter. 14.
This is the meaning: the "excellent mountain" (*varaḥ giriḥ*) is the supreme mountain Meru in the form of a skeleton. And so it is stated in the *Śrīsampuṭa*:
"The wind Bhairava, shaped like a bow, resides at the soles of the feet;
likewise, the extraction of the triangle resides in the region of the waist."
Varuṇa, indeed having a circular form, resides in the three petals;
and the Earth, likewise, is square in shape throughout the heart.

"For Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, is indeed in the form of a skeleton staff. Thus [it is said]. Its "cave" (*kandara*) is its hollow; that very [hollow] is profound because it is beyond the range of the five [senses]. To the question, "What occurs there?", he says: "There, the realm of selflessness (*nairātmyadhātu*), the entire world itself, having arisen, becomes stable. To the question, "What would result from this?", he says: "The stainless, which is of the nature of bliss through cessation, in the form of water—that is, in the form of the conventional fluid of semen—the stainless and equal *bodhicitta* undergoes drying up and falls downward. And so it is stated in the *Śukrasiddhi*, [which is surely the *Guhyasiddhi*]:
But when the thought of awakening— the treasury of all accomplishments— has fallen,
and the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be blameless accomplishment?

How is it that the fire of time (*kālāgni*) begins its course at the moment of entering the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣ� Mount Meru, the upholder of the earth; one does not find the unevenness [of the path]. Kṛṣṇa says: "Difficult to perceive, difficult to traverse—who can contemplate this within the mind? (15) [He] experiences the bliss of great passion (*mahārāga*) in the Unfallen (*acyuta*).

Thus he says: "This is that Mount Meru, the upholder of the earth; one does not find the unevenness [of the path]. Kṛṣṇa says: 'Difficult to perceive, difficult to traverse—who can contemplate this within the mind? (15)"

This is the meaning: this very beginner yogin, through the difficulty of suppressing the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, with a mind entirely motionless due to its immobility, does not indeed move; thus, the previously mentioned Meru—being "even and uneven" by way of the entry and exit of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*—likewise does not reach the northern peak of the upper Meru.

For this very reason, Kṛṣṇavajra says: because it is unperceived by the gods, uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others, and beyond the range of [ordinary] yogins, who can mentally perceive that supreme reality which is so difficult to fathom?
He whose mind is stirred by the nectar that vibrates naturally day and night—he alone knows the course of Dharma; what can others know, even if they speak?

He who realizes the jewel of the mind through the union of the thunderbolt and the lotus—the *bodhicitta* whose nature is non-emission, which is the innate (*sahaja*) essence manifest day and night—he alone is the supreme lord of yogins; he knows the reality of phenomena as it truly is, and no other who is attached to the pleasure characterized by the friction of the senses. Therefore, it is said: "By whom the binding of his own mind has been accomplished, by him the entire triple world is expanded and then withdrawn. (17)

The meaning is as follows: by that lord of yogins who has stabilized the *bodhicitta* in the form of vibration (*spanda*), the entire three worlds—in their nature of physical bliss (*kāyānanda*) and mental bliss (*cittānanda*)—are perceived as having vibrated forth without exception, and then, having been withdrawn again, they are made to enter into coemergent bliss (*sahajānanda*) and established within that which is designated as "bliss. Therefore, it is said: "O Goddess, where can one find the Tathāgatas? In what assembly of deities? Abiding in the moment of coemergence, free from the mandala-circle, I remain. (18)

This is the meaning. For what purpose? The connection is as follows: "Since the goddess Cittavajra-tathāgata is found within the host of wrathful deities, I abide in the moment of the innate (*sahaja*) [bliss], liberated from the maṇḍala-circle. If the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth—the deities of the maṇḍalas of body, speech, and mind—have attained the state of being of one flavor (*samarasībhāva*) through the instruction on great bliss, then this itself is the great maṇḍala; therefore, there is no separate maṇḍala other than this. Thus it is said in the *Guhyendutilaka Tantra*:
"Beyond the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its objects."
This supreme mandala is joined with the *mātrā* and the *bindu*. Thus [it is said].

O King of the Mind, he by whom the mind has been made motionless through the innate state of equal flavor (samarasa) becomes a Siddha at that very moment; indeed, there is no longer any fear of old age or death. 19.

This is the meaning: the connection is that by whatever yogin the bodhicitta—which is the fourth [joy] consisting of the bliss of gnosis—is made to become one flavor with the bodily bliss and so forth, in an unmoving and unswerving form through the means of innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*). By reaching the culmination of that practice, one arrives at the state of functioning; having abandoned aging and death in that very moment, one becomes a *siddha*. The meaning is that one effects the *mahāmudrā*. And so it is said in the *Śrī-samāja*: "At the time of the rising of the dawn, they attain accomplishment; there is no doubt about this. Clarifying that very point, he says: "Unmoving, free from conceptualization, free from wavering."
Utterly devoid of mental activity and possessing pure essence—
this is called Nirvāṇa,
wherein neither mind nor mentation performs anything whatsoever. || 20 ||

This is the meaning: it is called *nirvāṇa* because it is immovable due to being unshaken by the winds of all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*); non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) due to being free from [dualistic] seals (*mudrā*); changeless (*nirvikāra*) due to transcending the senses; and reaching the limit of arising (*udayānta*) due to being devoid of movement. It has a form like space, resembling the cloudless midday sky of autumn. In that state, the mind (*manas*), the consciousness (*citta*), and the eighty-four innate natures of the minds do not perform any action whatsoever. In such a state, no conceptualization of self, other, or both arises at all. This refers to the moment of the dawning of the luminous gnosis (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*).
He who has awakened to the syllable *evaṃ* has awakened to everything without exception; he alone is the casket of Dharma, O you whose dress is that of a self-proclaimed lord! 21.

This is the meaning. Regarding the term *evaṃkāra*: Mahāmudrā, whose nature is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion, is precisely this *evaṃkāra*. By that Lord of Yogins through whom this *evaṃkāra* is realized, the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and so forth, are realized. That very Mahāmudrā is the form of the casket of Dharma (*dharmakaraṇḍaka*) because she arises from the Dharmakāya. Therefore, she alone is the essence, the awakening, the dress, the ornament, the adornment, and the splendor of those [aggregates and so forth], which is to say, the attire of her own Lord, Vajradhara. And thus it is said in the Śrī Hevajra: "That divine form shaped like the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the letter *Vaṃ*."
The ālaya is the repository of all happiness and the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The letter *e* is the Mother, while the letter *va* is the Lord of Passion (*ratādhipa*).
The Bindu is the Unstruck Knowledge (*anāhata-jñāna*), and from it all other syllables are born."
If the gate of the wind’s movement is firmly barred,
and if the mind is made steadfast even in that terrible darkness.
O Jinarāja, if that supreme garment touches the belly, Kṛṣṇa says:
"Even while experiencing worldly existence, one attains liberation. 22.

This is the meaning: the gateway for the movement of the wind is there; at that point, this which is called "the indivisible" is the sealing of the two halves in an inseparable manner, whereby the paths of the moon and the sun are blocked. If, within that terrible darkness, the mental activity—the *bodhicitta*—is made into a fault because it illuminates great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then that jewel of the Victor touches the lower and upper lotuses known as the "excellent sky," namely the *avadhūtī*, and embraces it. To the question, "What would happen by this? he says:

Kṛṣṇavajra says: when that very existence is being experienced—that is, while one is enjoying the experience of the five qualities of sensual pleasure—nirvāṇa, the state of Mahāmudrā, becomes manifest.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"He who has made his mind truly immovable beholds the syllable of Dharma."
The wind is struck down at that very moment, and the poisons become powerless. || 23 ||

This is the meaning: that person, having made the mind—the *bodhicitta*—immovable through the union of the vajra and the lotus, also binds the wind, the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), to the side of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) consisting of the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) with the characteristics previously described. The meaning is that at that very moment, no other instant need be awaited, because of being free from the transformations of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). And so Saraha says: "Those elements have become utterly exhausted, since this very wind has become independent.
That passionate woman clings to the neck of her lover; even today, is she my friend for the sake of bodily pleasure?"
Now, one might ask: where is this syllable of Dharma to be known? It is perceived in the midst of the syllable of Dharma at that place where the two supreme cessations (paramavirama) are transcended.
If it is thus clearly realized that one attains perfection, then the wife of the wind (the breath) is bound motionless there. 24.

This is the meaning: disregard both supreme cessation (*paramavirama*) and passion-cessation (*rāgavirāga*), which consist of the forms of *kāla* and *vikāla*. Therein, for the purpose of establishing the instruction on the previously mentioned knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*)—which is the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*) characterized as the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśīkalā*) in the center—he says: "If, by such an instruction of the Mantra system, this knowledge-seal is clearly accomplished or perfected, then what happens? He says [the following]:

The meaning is that the steady [state] of that wife of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), who is the *jñānamudrā* in the form of a corpse (*śavarī*), is constrained—that is, she becomes motionless. Now, one might ask: "The corpse has indeed fallen; but what is the nature of the hunter (*śavara*), and where does he dwell? To this he says:
"On the peak of the excellent mountain, the lofty sage Śavara has made his dwelling. Even the lions do not leap over it, nor do the noble elephants cross it due to their ill fortune. (25)

That very Varagiri—meaning that same mountain peak (*śikhara-śṛṅga*) mentioned previously—is "high" (*uttuṅga*) because it is the support of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Regarding the dwelling made there by the Blessed One, the Śabara Vajradhara, the author asks: "By whom has it not been transgressed or stepped upon? [The answer is: "By the elephant-like vital wind (*prāṇapavana*) consisting of the five mandalas, the lordly elephant of the mind (*cittagajendra*); it is far beyond [their reach]. "This is that best of mountains, as described by me; this is that abode of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
In a single night, the moment of the innate (*sahaja*) is attained, for as long as there is great bliss. (26)

This is the meaning: that very best of mountains has been described by me as the Black Vajra (*kṛṣṇavajra*), and not described by anyone else; others like me are not capable of describing it. By way of exposition, this very place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is the aforementioned site (*sthalī*). Within this, produce that very Nirvāṇa characterized by great bliss until the state of the Vajra-holder (*vajradhara*), the lord of the fourteen stages, is attained. Anticipating the question, "Of what nature is this Vajra-holder?", he says: "The entire world, together with its bodies and minds, merges and flashes forth right here; it does not shine elsewhere."
Thus, in this dissolution, there is but one great bliss, which is Nirvāṇa. || 27 ||

This is the meaning: all those Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the rest, are the forms of the world by way of the nature of the five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*). Their body, speech, and mind exist in the form of earth and the other elements. When these are joined with the goddesses, Vairocanī and the others, they become one in a single mass as great passion (*mahārāga*) and so forth, characterized by perfect awakening—the body of the Vajradhara. Through the analogy of milk and water, there is a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) with these [elements]. Within that very body of Vajradhara, that same body, speech, mind, and so forth, radiate forth according to the analogy of waves upon water. By this, the meaning is that the triple world is the body of Vajradhara.
Not even a single mantra or tantra is effective against one who is sporting with his own wife at home.
As long as the mistress of the house does not bathe in her own home, how can one wander about adorned with the five colors? || 28 ||

This is its meaning: not even a single mantra is recited, nor is there the chanting of mantras, nor the study of the *tantra* according to the *tantra*. Having taken one's own wife as the *jñānamudrā*, who appears pure through the instruction of a true guru, the yogi should remain engaged in amorous play (*keli*) with her. And it has been said thus:
"Some [teachers] say that she is merely an appearance produced in the mind, like the reflection of the moon;
she is to be served by the lords of yogis and was served by the supreme sons of the Jina and by the Buddhas."
That flame of wisdom, having increased in intensity, burns away the entire host of Māra together with its objects;
and through the yoga of constant practice, it also burns away passion and the like within the body, bringing about the supreme bliss of the yogins.

"A yogin who is attached to this Blessed Lady should not engage in the grasping of mantras and tantras. His own wife is the form of Mahāmudrā; therein, she alone is the "housewife" (gṛhiṇī) of the Jñānamudrā. As long as one does not merge with or dissolve into her, what is accomplished by means of the five colors and forms? Demonstrating with certainty that the fruit of this very Mahāmudrā is the means for accomplishment, he says once more:
"This [is] recitation, fire-offering, and mandala-ritual;
Day after day you remain intent upon practicing the Dharma."
Without constant love for the Youthful One (Viṣṇu), can enlightenment be attained even with this very body? 29.

"O fool, why do you remain day after day with this external fire-sacrifice (*homa*) and the rites of the mandala? O deluded mind, in what manner [is this done]? How is all of this fruitless? Without her, one is always filled with passion; with the youthful *mahāmudrā*, there is delight and an uninterrupted affection within. Without that, how can the *mahāmudrā* be attained by means of this human body? Is it true that enlightenment (*bodhi*) cannot be achieved through another body once this human body has been abandoned?"
Why? Because of the statement: "Men are of the form of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣits. He states her fruit [as follows]:
"If one realizes even for a moment that rare innate state (sahaja), what need is there for the Vedas and Purāṇas?
By that, O friend, this entire world, with its measureless variety of poisons and dualities, is destroyed. (30)

By that [means] by which the nature of Mahāmudrā—the ever-arisen, innate characteristic—has been realized, the yogin has shattered and uprooted the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) of the mind along with all its conceptual constructions; this is the meaning.
"Having made the jewel of the mind motionless, one takes one's own wife here;
that is the 'thunderbolt' (vajra), O Lord, the supreme truth as spoken by me. (31)

This is the meaning: because it cannot be moved by any *pracaṇḍālī*, the jewel of the mind—the *bodhicitta*—is motionless; this very *divyamudrā* is one's own wife. In that very place, the *evaṃkāra*, the abode of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), he himself is the *Vajrī*, the Holder of the Vajra, the Lord, the master of body, speech, and mind. This supreme, uncontrived meaning has been stated by me, Kṛṣṇavajra. The meaning is that there is nothing other than this. Clarifying this very point, he says: "Just as salt dissolves in water, so the mind takes the wife."
If even the nectar of immortality were to become like that in an instant, it would still not equal it. 32.

This is the meaning: just as salt dissolves in water, so too the housewife, who is the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), takes hold of the mind and reaches a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) and single integration (*ekalolībhāva*). If at that very moment one remains eternally together with that housewife, whose form is the mind of bliss, then by this the Vajrasattvas of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*) are demonstrated. Thus ends the *Ācāryapādīya-dohā-koṣa-mekhalā-ṭīkā*.
